sources.content: Published 2026-03-04Updated 2026-06-23 Share: TL;DR: Linear alternatives ranked for engineering teams: 7 faster, cheaper, or open-source picks like Plane, Huly, and GitHub Issues. Pricing and fit compared. ## Why Look for Linear Alternatives? Linear earned its reputation by being the fastest, most opinionated issue tracker available. Its keyboard-first interface, automatic sprint management, and clean design make it a favorite among small-to-mid product and engineering teams. Where other tools offer maximum flexibility, Linear offers maximum velocity. [...] For teams that want to minimize their tool stack and maintain full data control, Huly's breadth is appealing. The issue tracking module is clean and fast, with customizable workflows, Kanban boards, and sprint management. The real-time collaboration features (chat, document editing, video calls) reduce the need for separate communication tools. Huly's ambition to be everything creates a predictable trade-off: each individual module is less deep than the dedicated tool it replaces. The issue tracker is good but not as polished as Linear. [...] Jira is the industry standard for issue tracking, and it represents the opposite end of the philosophy spectrum from Linear. Where Linear constrains workflows for speed, Jira allows nearly unlimited customization: custom issue types, fields, workflows, screens, permission schemes, and automation rules. If you can describe a process, Jira can model it. For product teams in larger organizations (100+ engineers), Jira's advantages are real. Cross-project reporting, advanced roadmaps (formerly Portfolio), and the Atlassian ecosystem (Confluence, Bitbucket, Opsgenie) create an integrated development operations platform. sources.title: GitHub Status
sources.content: Resolved - On October 7, 2026, GitHub had two outages of write operations with the same cause, totaling about 19 minutes. The first ran from 15:06 to 15:16 UTC (about 10 minutes) and the second from 16:52 to 17:01 UTC (about 9 minutes). In both windows, actions that save or change data failed across Git operations, pull requests, issues, GitHub Actions, the API, webhooks, sign-in and authentication, GitHub Apps and OAuth, code scanning, Codespaces, and Copilot. Reading data was largely unaffected. [...] Resolved - On October 6, 2026, from 19:44 to 19:50 UTC, GitHub experienced a service outage with elevated error rates peaking at 1.30% of all requests, totaling approximately 1.16 million failed requests. This impacted 12 services across GitHub, including Pull Requests, Webhooks, Repos, OAuth, Git over SSH, Codespaces, and Gists. The incident was triggered by GitHub Enterprise Importer (GEI) making multiple, long duration queries which saturated a database connection pool. Recovery was seen at approximately 19:50 UTC once the migration's calls stopped; GEI migrations were reenabled at 23:32 UTC after a code fix was merged. [...] In the first outage, 5.6% of all web and API requests failed, peaking at 8.9%, and more than 12,000 organizations saw failed requests. Up to 26% of Git authentication requests failed, and 17% of Actions workflow runs failed with infrastructure errors. In the second outage, 6.2% of web and API requests failed, peaking at 9.3%, and more than 11,000 organizations were affected. Up to 25% of Git authentication requests failed, and 19% of Actions workflow runs failed. No databases experienced data loss, and operations retried after recovery succeeded.

sources.title: What Does it Mean When Your GitHub Issue is Closed, and What Can You Do? - Yihui Xie | 谢益辉
sources.content: In short, when I don’t have time, and the workaround is not awfully bad or complicated, I tend to close the issue, so I can move on to other issues—there are so many after all. A closed issue does not necessarily mean that it is invalid, but often means that it is not manageable under all the constraints. However, it is possible that my evaluation of the workaround is wrong. It might be okay or easy in my eyes, but bad or complicated in your opinion. Therefore I don’t mean that once an issue is closed, the request is denied forever. You could continue to argue and I could reopen it later. Sometimes I do make mistakes in my judgment, and sometimes you may have walked into my blind spots. I’ll be happy to reconsider the requests or correct my mistakes even years later. [...] Usually I try hard not to close issues without a response. I did close a few out of the thousands of issues that I have dealt with over the years, but these ones were often far below the minimum requirements, e.g., an issue with no content but only a brief title that I don’t completely understand, or an issue asking a random question that is completely irrelevant to the GitHub repo. Normally I do not even close issues right away that lack minimum reproducible examples, although that requirement is mentioned in the issue guide and should be seen when a new issue is opened. The most common reason why I close issues without fulfilling the original requests is the combination of the two conditions below: [...] So you may need some persistence if you feel I really missed anything in your request. BTW, if you want to learn what a terribly stubborn person I am, check out the hugo issue #3632 (perhaps someday I’ll just give it up, since I’ve already found a workaround in blogdown). sources.content: Tupolev Tu-154M landing Mikhalis Makarov/Shutterstock Russia's last commercial Tupolev Tu-154 was finally retired from service in 2020, almost half a century after the first one left the factory. Production of the jet began in 1972, just as the then-Soviet Union's domestic aviation industry was starting to rapidly expand. The Tu-154 formed a vital part of that expansion, and was a common sight in the country's skies all the way through to the 2000s. It remained in production until 2013, but by that time, Russia's airlines had already largely replaced the jet with more modern, fuel-efficient aircraft from Airbus and Boeing. [...] It was announced in 2019 that production of the A380 would end, since the demand simply wasn't there to keep the production line open. Most airlines instead favored the twin-jet A350, which could carry almost as many passengers but was notably cheaper to run. Thanks to their inherent inefficiency and limited versatility, many A380 aircraft were sent into retirement as the effects of the pandemic plunged many operators into losses. However, with the post-pandemic travel boom, many are now returning to service and are expected to remain in the skies for the next decade or more. ## Concorde Concorde 001 at launch Victor Drees/Getty Images [...] The 757's design also made it less practical to update, with more significant –- and therefore costly –- revisions needed for it to become as efficient as market-leading models. sources.title: Double-Decker Planes Dead After Airbus A380, Boeing 747 Stop Production - Business Insider
sources.content: It's the end of an era for four-engined planes. Boeing is stopping production of its famed 747 aircraft by 2023 and Airbus just trucked its last A380 fuselage through France in June as it prepares to shut down the line in 2021 after less than two decades of production. Both were a casualty of weak demand from the airlines they faithfully served amid a crippling pandemic, though their popularity began to wane long before the first COVID-19 case was reported. [...] The once-long-haul leaders are now being put out to pasture and the coronavirus pandemic is only speeding that process along. Qantas, KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, Virgin Atlantic Airways, and Corsair have all retired their Boeing 747s months ahead of schedule while Air France abruptly retired its Airbus A380 fleet in May, 11 years after its first flight for the flag carrier. It wasn't for lack of comfort, as most travelers loved the additional space offered by both aircraft, which allowed for amenities not found on most single-engine jets. The early days of the 747 saw the iconic hump used for cocktail lounges or a restaurant in the skies while the A380 is known for being the only commercial airliner to have an in-flight shower, which Emirates offers to first class passengers. [...] All Nippon Airways was the last new airline to take delivery of the Airbus A380 in March 2019 and while the manufacturer had likely hoped the iconic jet would be saved by another new order, the coronavirus pandemic ensured that wouldn't happen. Emirates will be the last customer to take delivery of the jet that may roam the skies for another two decades before the last of its kind is retired. Unlike its Boeing counterpart, the A380 has not been able to make the transition into the cargo realm, except for one airline that hollowed out its sole A380 to increase cargo capacity during the COVID-19 airlift. There are few uses for secondhand A380s, with demand undoubtedly dropping even more with the pandemic.

sources.title: What is Linear Pricing? Definition | oboloo Blog
sources.content: Linear pricing is a pricing strategy where price increases or decreases in direct proportion to the quantity of goods or services purchased. This type of pricing is common in businesses that sell commodities or other undifferentiated products. While linear pricing is straightforward and easy to understand, it can often be perceived as unfair by customers. This is because customers who purchase more of a product are effectively subsidizing the cost for those who purchase less. Linear pricing can also be difficult to sustain in cases where the cost of production decreases with increased output. In these situations, companies may find themselves selling at a loss if they do not adjust their prices accordingly. Despite these challenges, linear pricing remains a popular pricing strategy due to [...] ## What is Linear Pricing? Linear pricing is a pricing strategy in which companies charge a consistent price for their goods or services, regardless of demand. This type of pricing is common in industries where there is little to no competition and where customers are less price-sensitive. Some examples of industries that typically use linear pricing are utilities (e.g., electricity, water, gas), public transportation (e.g., buses, trains, subways), and garbage collection. In these industries, it is difficult for customers to switch to another provider, so companies can get away with charging a higher price when demand is high. [...] ## Pros and Cons of Linear Pricing Linear pricing is a type of pricing strategy where the price of a product or service is based on the quantity of units sold. This means that each unit sold has the same price, regardless of how many units are sold. linear pricing can be used to encourage customers to buy more products or services, as they know that they will get the same price per unit regardless of how many units they purchase.

sources.title: Linear vs GitHub Issues vs Jira (2026) | DevToolReviews
sources.content: Linear, GitHub Issues, and Jira represent three philosophies: Linear optimizes for speed and opinionated workflows, GitHub Issues integrates tightly with code, and Jira offers maximum configurability for complex organizations. We used all three on active projects over four weeks. ## Speed and Responsiveness This is Linear's defining advantage. The application loads instantly, transitions are animated at 60fps, and every action — creating an issue, changing status, filtering, searching — responds in under 100ms. Linear achieves this through aggressive local caching and optimistic updates. When you drag an issue to a new status, the UI updates immediately; the server sync happens in the background. [...] ## The Verdict Linear is the best project management tool for small-to-medium engineering teams in 2026. Its speed, keyboard-driven workflow, and opinionated design make daily issue tracking feel effortless rather than burdensome. GitHub Issues is the right choice for open-source projects and cost-conscious teams that value code integration over workflow features. Jira remains the enterprise standard — its configurability and reporting depth are unmatched, even if its speed and usability lag behind Linear. [...] ## Reporting and Analytics Jira offers the most comprehensive reporting: velocity charts, burndown charts, cumulative flow diagrams, sprint reports, and custom JQL-powered dashboards. For organizations that need to report engineering metrics to stakeholders, Jira provides the most out of the box. Linear provides cycle reports (velocity, scope changes), project progress tracking, and team analytics. The reports are clean and actionable but less customizable than Jira's. GitHub Issues has minimal built-in reporting. sources.title: We Outgrew GitHub Issues at 500 Tickets. Linear Was the Obvious Next Step.
sources.content: The standup generator works because Linear's data model is clean. Every state change, comment, and assignment is tracked in the issue activity. The agent reads that activity stream and composes a readable summary. In GitHub Issues, the equivalent data exists in the timeline but it's mixed with CI events, PR reviews, and deployment notifications. Priya also uses a sprint status reporter that generates Friday summaries with completion rates and velocity trends. She forwards it to leadership without editing it most weeks. Neither GitHub Issues nor Linear's native features can analyze sprint data and write a narrative about what it means. Agents handle that layer. ## The Decision Framework [...] The proximity to code. In GitHub Issues, you're already in the repo. You can reference a line of code, link to a file, and see the code context without switching tools. In Linear, you're in a separate application. The code lives in GitHub. The issues live in Linear. The two are connected by links and integrations, but they're not in the same place. For debugging sessions where you're jumping between code and issues, the context switch is real. Free. GitHub Issues costs nothing. Linear is $8 per user per month. For a ten-person team, that's $960 per year. Not much, but GitHub Issues is literally free. For pre-revenue startups counting every dollar, the zero cost of GitHub Issues is meaningful. ## The Agent Layer [...] ## What Changed Immediately The speed difference was the first thing everyone noticed. Linear's local sync engine means the interface responds instantly. Clicking on an issue loads it in under 100 milliseconds because the data is already cached on your machine. GitHub Issues requires a server round trip for every page load. The difference in absolute time is small (maybe one to two seconds per interaction), but at dozens of interactions per day, it changes the experience from "using a web app" to "using a desktop app."

sources.title: Creating the Ideal Team Workflow with Linear and Github
sources.content: Slack: You can create issues from Slack and sync discussions across both platforms. This allows you to keep track of discussions and tasks directly within Slack, making it easier to collaborate with your team members. GitHub: By linking your issues to GitHub, you can automate your pull request workflows. This means that status changes in GitHub will be automatically updated in Linear, saving you time and effort. You can also link single or multiple issues to a specific pull request, and comments in Linear will be synced with GitHub conversations.

sources.title: Linear Review (2026): Pricing, Pros & Cons, Verdict | Siit
sources.content: Linear Agent: Launched in public beta on March 24, 2026 and free on all plans during beta, agents are full workspace members that can be assigned to issues, added to projects, or mentioned in comments to triage, answer questions, create follow-up work, and draft project updates. Shared Skills (June 4, 2026) let teams save and reuse agent instructions. Coding Sessions: Generally available June 11, 2026 on Basic, Business, and Enterprise (AI credits required), where Linear Agent writes code using Claude Code and Codex, running in the cloud with workspace context so teams can prototype without local setup. [...] TL;DR verdict: Linear is a fast, minimalist product development system built for software teams, with speed and developer-first UX as its standout strengths and workflow rigidity as its main limitation. Teams that live in issues and PRs get the most from it; teams that need client-facing reporting or deep customization across departments should look elsewhere. Ratings: G2: 4.6/5 · Capterra: 4.3/5, verified August 2026 ## What Is Linear? [...] Linear Diffs: The code-review feature, available on all plans since May 28, 2026, lets teams review PR diffs from any issue and ship without leaving Linear, syncing back to GitHub; Business and Enterprise add Guided Reviews that explain each section of a diff. Loops: Launched July 20, 2026 on Business and Enterprise (AI credits required), Loops are recurring agent automations that run on a schedule or in response to an event, described in plain language.

sources.title: Changelog – Linear
sources.content: Skip to content → AllChangelogProduct launchesFrom the teamFrom the communityPress June 11, 2026 ## Coding sessions in Linear Earlier this year, we launched Linear Agent, giving teams a new way to plan and coordinate their issues and projects. Since then, we’ve added Code Intelligence to extend that understanding to the codebase, and MCP support to bring all of your context together. Today we’re closing the loop: Linear Agent can now write code using Claude Code and Codex. You can triage, plan, review, and ship—all in Linear. Start a coding session by assigning an issue to Linear, or ask it to make a change in a chat, comment, or Slack thread. Each session is grounded in your workspace context, pulling in issue details, history, customer requests, discussions, and related work.

sources.title: Linear for Mac (2026) — Review & Install — Bundl.run
sources.content: Bundl Submit an App Linear icon # Linear Modern issue tracking and project management For Mac Official website Free + paid plans Editorial score 4.7/5 Bundl review CategoryProductivity PlatformmacOS InstallationHomebrew ## Preview Take a closer look Website previewCredit: Linear ## Our review 4.7/5 Bundl editorial assessment How we review apps Linear in August 2026 is still the default modern issue tracker for product-engineering teams that value speed: Free for evaluation, Basic at $10, Business at $16, and a serious agent story on top. The Free 250-issue cap and annual paid billing are the main frictions. If you need Jira-level flexibility, look elsewhere. If you want low tracker latency and agents in the loop, Linear remains outstanding. ### Best for [...] Linear is a modern issue tracker and product delivery platform for software teams that prefer speed over endless configuration. It syncs data for a local-first feel, leans hard on keyboard workflows, and pairs issues with projects, cycles, initiatives, plus an expanding agent platform. As of August 2026 Linear reports trust from more than 40,000 companies and keeps pushing AI: Linear Agent, triage intelligence, coding sessions, loops, and MCP access show up across marketing and CEO/COO updates. Some AI features are metered via AI credits instead of a flat AI seat tax. Pricing on linear.app/pricing (verified August 2026): - Free, $0: unlimited members, 2 teams, 250 issues, agent platform / Linear Agent entry points, 10MB file uploads. - Basic, $10 per user/month (billed yearly): 5 teams, [...] Verified against linear.app/pricing in August 2026. - Free ($0): Unlimited members; 2 teams; 250 issues; agent platform & Linear Agent; 10MB uploads; core issues/projects/cycles/initiatives. - Basic ($10/user/month, billed yearly): 5 teams; unlimited issues; unlimited uploads; admin roles; all Free features. - Business ($16/user/month, billed yearly): Unlimited teams; private teams & guests; Triage Intelligence; Loops; Code Intelligence (beta); Insights; Asks; Zendesk/Intercom integrations; advanced AI/agent workflows (some require AI credits). - Enterprise (custom, annual): SAML & SCIM; granular admin; advanced security; invoice/PO; migration & onboarding support; priority support; account management. Notes: Marketing emphasizes yearly billing for paid seats. Certain agent/coding session

sources.title: Best project management software for startups in 2026
sources.content: ## Engineering trackers ### Linear Linear issue list with Todo issues, sidebar for teams, projects and views Pricing: Free for unlimited members, capped at 2 teams and 250 issues. Basic is $10 per user per month and Business $16, both billed yearly; Linear's pricing page shows yearly rates only. Guest accounts need Business and are billed as regular members. Coding sessions and Loops draw on prepaid AI credits, while Linear's other AI features are included in the plan. Rating: 4.6/5 on G2 from 122 reviews, 4.4/5 on Capterra from 5 reviews.

supported_claims.text: Linear offers a free plan.
Linear’s free plan supports unlimited members and is capped at 2 teams and 250 issues.
Linear’s Basic plan costs $10 per user per month as of July 2026.
Linear’s Business plan costs $16 per user per month as of July 2026.
Linear’s Enterprise plan uses custom pricing.
Linear’s paid plans for organizations range from $5,000 to $70,000 annually based on needs.
Annual billing typically offers a discount compared to month-to-month billing.
Guest accounts require the Business plan and are billed as regular members.
Linear’s Business plan includes priority support, advanced analytics, SAML SSO, and SCIM provisioning.
Linear’s Enterprise plan includes dedicated support, advanced security, and compliance features.
Linear’s Coding Sessions and Loops draw on prepaid AI credits, while other AI features are included in the plan.
Coding Sessions are available on Linear’s Basic, Business, and Enterprise plans.
Linear is described as the fastest, most opinionated issue tracker available with a keyboard-first interface.
Linear features automatic sprint management.
Linear is a favorite among small-to-mid product and engineering teams.
Linear is described as the best issue tracker for most engineering teams in 2026.
Linear competes with alternatives including GitHub Issues, Jira, Height, Plane, Huly, and OpenProject.
The application loads instantly and actions respond in under 100ms.
GitHub Issues is identified as the clear choice for open-source projects and teams working entirely within GitHub.
Jira is identified as the choice for enterprises needing unlimited configurability and formal Scrum analytics.
Linear provides a cleaner data model than GitHub Issues, with state changes tracked directly in issue activity.
Linear integrates with GitHub to automatically update issue statuses and sync comments with pull requests.
Linear and GitHub Issues both support MCP servers.
Linear supports delegation to agents including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Devin.
Linear holds a Bundl editorial score of 4.7 out of 5 as of August 2026.
Linear holds a G2 rating of 4.6 out of 5 based on 122 reviews.
Linear holds a Capterra rating of 4.4 out of 5 based on 5 reviews.
Linear Agent entered public beta on March 24, 2026, and was free on all plans during beta.
Linear introduced Shared Skills on June 4, 2026.
Linear’s Coding Sessions feature became generally available on June 11, 2026.
Linear was described in August 2026 as "the default modern issue tracker for product-engineering teams that value speed."
